definition: In image processing, a steerable filter is an orientation-selective filter that can be computationally rotated to any direction.
details: Rather than designing a new filter for each orientation, a steerable filter is synthesized from a linear combination of a small, fixed set of "basis filters". This approach is efficient and is widely used for tasks that involve directionality, such as edge detection, texture analysis, and shape-from-shading. The principle of steerability has been generalized in deep learning to create equivariant neural networks, which can recognize features in data regardless of their orientation or position.

explainer.lead: A steerable filter is an orientation-selective image filter that can be computationally rotated to any direction. It matters because any orientation is synthesised from a small fixed set of basis filters instead of designing a new filter each time.

tiers.eli5: Instead of making a separate stencil for every possible angle, you keep a few stencils and blend them to point wherever you want.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use steerable filters for edge detection, texture analysis and shape-from-shading, rotating the filter cheaply rather than redesigning it. A pitfall is that only orientations spanned by the fixed basis filters can be synthesised.
tiers.paperLevel: An orientation-selective filter synthesized as a linear combination of a small, fixed set of basis filters, allowing computational rotation to any direction. The principle has been generalized in deep learning to equivariant neural networks that recognize features regardless of orientation or position.

explainer.example: An edge detector is steered to a chosen angle by combining basis filter responses, so edges at that orientation respond strongly.
